The lighthouse appeared in the wheat field sometime between the evening weather report and the first bus to town.

It was not an especially handsome lighthouse. Its white paint had blistered, and rust ran down from the gallery railing in long, apologetic streaks. Someone had left a mop outside the door. At its base, the wheat leaned away in a perfect circle, as though politely making room.

Our nearest ocean was six hundred miles east.

By seven, people had parked along the county road to look. By eight, someone was selling coffee. By nine, the farmer, Mr. Bell, had put up a sign:

**PLEASE DO NOT WALK ON THE CROP TO INVESTIGATE THE IMPOSSIBLE.**

I arrived at ten because the town employed me to inspect structures, and whatever else it was, the lighthouse was plainly a structure.

Mr. Bell met me at the fence.

“Is it yours?” I asked.

“Do I look like I ordered a lighthouse?”

“People order unusual things.”

“Last thing I ordered was a replacement belt for the combine. They sent the wrong belt. This is worse.”

I ducked between the wires.

Up close, the tower smelled of salt and old pennies. There was a brass knocker shaped like a fish. Beneath it, a small notice read:

**KEEPER TEMPORARILY ABSENT.  
PLEASE MAINTAIN THE LIGHT.**

The door was unlocked.

Inside stood a narrow bed, a table, a stove, and a pair of rubber boots placed neatly on yesterday’s newspaper. The newspaper was from a town I had never heard of. Its lead story concerned a missing lighthouse.

I folded it and put it in my bag.

Then I climbed.

There were eighty-three steps. I counted because counting is one of the few things you can do professionally while afraid.

At the top, an enormous lens surrounded a lamp no larger than a mixing bowl. Everything was clean. The brass shone. A logbook lay open on a stool.

The latest entry said:

*Tuesday. Fog. Nothing lost.*

Below that:

*Wednesday. Clear. Nothing lost.*

Below that, in a shakier hand:

*Thursday. Inland. Will inquire.*

I looked out across the wheat.

From that height, our town seemed both smaller and more complicated. I could see the water tower, the school roof, the pale rectangle where the grocery store had burned down. Cars collected around the lighthouse like filings around a magnet.

There was a switch beside the lamp.

I left it alone.

***

By afternoon, the mayor wanted it removed.

By evening, the historical society wanted it preserved.

The school principal wanted to know whether children could visit, and the insurance company wanted everyone to stop using the word *appeared*.

I wrote a preliminary report.

*Foundation inaccessible. Staircase sound. Electrical supply undetermined. Recommend no immediate action.*

This was not cowardice. “No immediate action” is often the most useful thing a town employee can recommend.

That night, I went back.

I told myself I wanted to check the wiring. In fact, I had been thinking about the notice on the door.

*Please maintain the light.*

There are instructions you can ignore all day that become difficult after dark.

The coffee seller had gone home. Mr. Bell’s sign moved softly in the wind. I crossed the field with a flashlight, found the door, and climbed the eighty-three steps.

Then I turned the switch.

The lamp lit without a sound.

Its beam passed over the wheat, the road, the town. It swept across the church steeple and the supermarket loading dock. It entered bedroom windows and crossed kitchen tables.

On its third circuit, my phone rang.

It was my sister.

“Are you at the lighthouse?”

“Yes.”

“Can you leave it on?”

I waited.

“Just for a while,” she said.

My sister had spent the past month packing up her house. Her husband had left in January, and she was trying to decide whether leaving town would count as starting over or merely leaving town.

“Does it bother you?” I asked.

“No,” she said. “That’s the thing.”

***

Other people called.

A nurse finishing her shift asked who had authorized it. When I apologized, she said she hadn’t complained.

A boy watching his little brother while their mother worked sent the town’s public information account a photograph of the beam crossing their ceiling.

Mr. Bell called at eleven.

“It comes through my window every forty seconds.”

“I can turn it off.”

He was quiet.

“Didn’t say that.”

I stayed until dawn.

***

The keeper returned on Saturday.

She was short, sunburned, and carrying a canvas bag full of oranges.

“Any trouble?” she asked.

“Some.”

“Usually is.”

She set the oranges on the table and inspected the stove.

“Where did you go?” I asked.

“To ask directions.”

“From whom?”

She gave me a look that suggested I was not licensed to inspect that question.

Outside, wind moved through the wheat in broad, traveling shadows.

“Will it go back?” I asked.

“Oh, yes.”

“When?”

“When we can.”

I wanted to ask what that meant. Instead I asked whether she needed anything.

“Fresh bread,” she said. “And the bottom stair has a wobble.”

***

The lighthouse vanished the following Monday.

It left a round patch of flattened wheat and one orange, which Mr. Bell found beneath his tractor.

For several nights afterward, I woke every forty seconds, or imagined I did.

My sister stayed in town. She said rent was cheaper here.

At the next council meeting, I submitted a modest proposal: replace the broken lights at the bus shelter, repaint the hospital entrance, and put a reflective marker on the dangerous bend beyond the school.

The mayor asked what had prompted this.

I said I had noticed some maintenance issues while working nights.

The motion passed, four votes to two.
